items.title: Why a token 20 seconds past exp still works
items.body:
JwtBearer validates the lifetime with a tolerance called `ClockSkew`. Its library default is five minutes; Bazaar sets it to 30 seconds. A token is rejected only once the current time is later than `exp` plus the skew, so 20 seconds past `exp` is still inside the window and the request is accepted.

- ClockSkew is 30 seconds in this file, not zero.
- Lifetime checks apply the configured skew; there is no zero-tolerance mode here.
- Nothing in the API reissues or refreshes tokens; the client must sign in again after the window.

items.title: Why the discount does not lower the tax
items.body:
The tax lines are built from `Price.Amount * Quantity` for each active line, and `CalculateTaxAsync` runs before the discount code is even loaded. With one 100.00 line at 10%, tax is 10.00, whatever the code takes off later. ADR 0002 records tax on the pre-discount amount as a deliberate choice.

- 9.00 would need tax on the discounted 90.00; the code never passes that amount.
- 8.25% is the fallback for an address with no zone, and here a zone matches.
- Shipping is not a tax line, so it adds no tax.

excerpts.quote: Tax is charged on the pre-discount amount (a deliberate, documented choice).

items.title: Why the discounted cart still ships free
items.body:
Shipping is priced on line 122, from `subtotal`, before the discount code is loaded on the lines after it. For a `FreeOverThreshold` method, `CalculateCost` returns zero when `subtotal.Amount >= threshold`. The subtotal is 80.00, and 80.00 is at least 75.00, so shipping is free even though the customer pays for only 60.00 of goods.

- The 60.00 figure is never passed to the shipping method.
- A gift card is tendered last and has no effect on shipping.
- No proration exists; the method returns either its base rate or zero.

excerpts.quote: var shipping = method?.CalculateCost(subtotal, itemCount, totalWeightGrams) ?? Money.Zero(currency);

items.title: Why a valid customer token gets 403 on admin routes
items.body:
The Admin policy chains `RequireAuthenticatedUser()` and `RequireRole` for the Admin role. A valid Customer token passes authentication, so the user is known; the role requirement then fails, and ASP.NET Core answers 403 Forbidden. A caller with no token at all fails authentication and gets 401. ADR 0006 states both outcomes.

- 401 is for an unauthenticated caller, and this caller is authenticated.
- 404 is used for another customer's resources, not for admin endpoints.
- The role is written under the standard `ClaimTypes.Role` key, so the token is not malformed.

excerpts.quote: a valid token whose role is not `Admin` (or that carries no role) is **403**; a guest is **401**.

items.title: Concept: rounding rules and the order of totals
items.body:
Money code has two decisions that change the cents on every order.

**Rounding.** When an amount lands exactly halfway between two cents, a program must pick a rule. Half away from zero sends 0.5 up; half to even sends it to the nearest even digit, so ties go up and down equally often over many sums. C# picks the rule through the `MidpointRounding` argument of `decimal.Round`. Open `Money.cs` and the cents converter, find the argument each one passes, and work one example of your own that ends in exactly half a cent.

**Order of steps.** Subtotal, tax, shipping, discount and gift card can be applied in different orders, and each order gives a different total. For each step in `CheckoutAsync`, write down which amount it receives: the raw line amounts, the subtotal, or the subtotal after the discount. Then check `ZoneTaxService` for what it does when no zone matches, and `ShippingMethod.CalculateCost` for what it compares against a threshold.

ADR 0002 and ADR 0011 state the intended rules; the code is the final word.

excerpts.quote: The order these apply in changes the amounts, so it must be fixed and explicit.

items.title: Why two simultaneous checkouts can end in a 500
items.body:
The order number is `BZ-{1001 + count}`, read with `CountAsync` before the save. Two checkouts that both count 5 orders both build BZ-1006. `Order.Number` has a unique index, so the slower save fails with a `DbUpdateException` from the constraint. `GlobalExceptionHandler` special-cases only `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`; this exception is its base class, not that subtype, so the response is a 500. The charge ran before the save, so the shopper paid for an order that was never written. This is a real bug in the repository.

- No concurrency token is involved, so there is no 409.
- Numbers are not a database sequence.
- Nothing refunds the charge, and no 402 is sent.

items.title: Why 0.125 of tax is stored as 0.12
items.body:
`ZoneTaxService` adds up `amount * rate` with full decimal precision (2.50 times 0.05 is 0.125) and wraps the sum in `new Money(tax, currency)`. The `Money` constructor rounds with `MidpointRounding.ToEven`: a value exactly halfway rounds to the even cent, so 0.125 becomes 0.12. The cents converter also rounds to even, and it receives 0.12 already.

- 0.13 is what half away from zero would give; this code does not use that mode.
- Money never keeps more than two decimals; the constructor rounds every value.
- The converter does not round up; it uses the same to-even rule on an amount already in cents.

items.title: Why a declined charge leaves no rows behind
items.body:
Everything checkout does before the charge is in memory: `Reserve` changes tracked `InventoryItem` objects, and the `Order` is built but not yet added to the context. On a decline the method returns `CheckoutOutcome.Fail` straight away. `_db.Orders.Add` and the single `SaveChangesAsync` come later, so nothing is written, and the request's DbContext is discarded with its pending changes.

- No Pending order exists to retry; it was never added.
- There is no reservation table or sweeper; reservations are per-request and in memory.
- No Cancelled audit row is written for a decline.

excerpts.quote: On a decline, return early **without** saving — the in-memory reservation evaporates.

items.title: When the concurrency stamp changes
items.body:
Both `SaveChanges` overrides call `RefreshConcurrencyStamps` first. It walks every tracked `IConcurrencyStamped` entry and gives a fresh `Guid` only to entries whose state is `Modified`. EF keeps the original stamp it loaded and puts it in the UPDATE's `WHERE`; if another writer has changed the stamp in the meantime, no row matches and EF throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`.

- Inserts are not restamped by this method; the stamp changes on later modifications.
- Reads never change the stamp.
- There is no database trigger; the stamp is set in C# before the save.

items.title: What happens when no tax zone matches
items.body:
`ZoneTaxService` looks for a region match, then a country-wide zone. If neither exists, `zone` is null, so `zone?.RateFor(...)` is null and the `??` picks `FallbackRate`, which is `FlatRateTaxCalculator.Rate`, 8.25%. Each line is taxed at that rate. The guide explains why: addresses without a zone reproduce the totals of orders placed before zones existed.

- An unmatched address is not tax-free in this code.
- No nearest-zone search exists; zones are filtered by the address country.
- Nothing fails: the fallback is the normal path for a zone-less address.

items.title: Why one Money object cannot fill two owned columns
items.body:
`Money` is mapped as an owned type, and EF Core tracks owned entities per object instance, attached to one owner navigation. Putting the same instance in two navigations asks EF to track one object as two owned entities, and the guide says EF throws. That is why `AmountToApply`, `Redeem` and `Restore` build a new `Money` each time.

- Record value equality does not help: tracking is by instance, not by `Equals`.
- EF does not silently zero a column to resolve the conflict.
- The guide puts the failure in EF's owned-type tracking, not in a SQLite constraint.

excerpts.quote: EF Core owned-type tracking keys on the *object instance*.
// Always a fresh Money instance so callers can assign it to a separate owned navigation.

items.title: How many webhook sends a failing endpoint gets
items.body:
`MaxAttempts` is 3 and the loop runs while `attempts < MaxAttempts && !success`, so a URL that always fails is sent three times in a row with no delay. After the loop the dispatcher adds one `WebhookDelivery` for that subscription, with `AttemptCount = attempts`. The docs say up to three retries and that every attempt is recorded; the code makes three attempts in total and keeps one summary row.

- Three retries after a first send would be four sends; the loop stops at three.
- Retries are inline in the request, not in a background job.
- Attempts are counted on one row, not stored one row each.

items.title: How a 10.05 refund splits between card and gift card
items.body:
`SplitRefundByTender` computes `cardShare = (grand - giftCardTendered) / grand`, here (20.00 - 10.00) / 20.00 = 0.5. The card refund is `new Money(10.05 * 0.5)`, which is 5.025 before rounding; the `Money` constructor rounds half to even, giving 5.02. The gift card gets the exact remainder, 10.05 - 5.02 = 5.03, so the cents add up to the full refund.

- 5.03 to the gateway would need half-away-from-zero rounding.
- The gateway is not refunded the whole amount; the split is proportional.
- The gift card is not refunded first; both shares come from one formula.
